section.title: Habakkuk's Second Complaint
section.sectionRationale: God's answer in the first movement, that He will raise up Babylon, only sharpens the prophet's problem: how can a holy God use a nation more wicked than the one He is judging? This second complaint presses that harder question, and it ends with Habakkuk climbing his watchtower to wait for God's reply, which sets up the great answer of chapter two.
section.thesis: Faced with God's plan to judge Judah by a crueler Babylon, Habakkuk clings to God's holiness and eternity, protests that the wicked seem to swallow the more righteous, and then takes his stand on the watchtower to wait for God's answer.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the second complaint, You are holy and eternal, so how can You use the treacherous to devour the righteous; and the prophet's resolve, I will stand at my watch and wait to see what God will say.

units.label: The harder question
units.note: how can a holy God use the wicked

verses.text: Are You not from everlasting, O LORD, my God, my {{qadosh|Holy One}}? We will not die. O LORD, You have appointed them to execute judgment; O {{tsur|Rock}}, You have established them for correction.

Your eyes are {{tahor|too pure}} to look upon evil, and You cannot tolerate wrongdoing. So why do You tolerate the faithless? Why are You silent while the wicked swallow up those more righteous than themselves?
You have made men like the fish of the sea, like creeping things that have no ruler.
The foe pulls all of them up with a hook; he catches them in his dragnet, and gathers them in his fishing net; so he rejoices gladly.
Therefore he sacrifices to his dragnet and burns incense to his fishing net, for by these things his portion is sumptuous and his food is rich.
Will he, therefore, empty his net and continue to slay nations without mercy?

units.label: The prophet on the watchtower
units.note: I will wait to see what He will say

verses.text: I will stand at my {{mishmereth|guard post}} and station myself on the ramparts. I will watch to see what He will say to me, and how I should answer when corrected.

qadosh.gloss: Holy, set apart, utterly pure. To call God the Holy One is to confess His moral perfection and separateness from all sin. Habakkuk anchors his whole complaint here: because God is holy, evil is a problem that demands an answer.

tsur.gloss: Rock, a picture of God as the unshakable, dependable refuge and foundation of His people. Even while protesting, Habakkuk addresses God as Rock, holding onto the stability of God's character in the middle of his confusion.

tahor.gloss: Pure, clean, without defilement. Habakkuk says God's eyes are too pure to look upon evil, that is, God cannot regard wickedness with approval or indifference. This purity is exactly what makes God's use of wicked Babylon so hard to understand.

mishmereth.gloss: A watch, guard post, or place of keeping. Habakkuk pictures himself as a watchman climbing to his post to look out for God's reply. It is the posture of active, expectant waiting: he has spoken his complaint and now stations himself to hear God answer.

basic.context: God has just told Habakkuk that He will deal with Judah's sin by sending Babylon. But that answer creates a bigger problem for the prophet. Babylon is even more wicked than Judah. So how can a perfectly holy God use a crueler nation to punish a less cruel one? Habakkuk lays this out, comparing Babylon to a fisherman who hauls in whole nations with his net and then worships the net. Then, instead of storming off, he climbs his watchtower to wait for God to reply.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a model of how to wrestle with God rightly. Habakkuk does not deny God's character; he actually builds his argument on it, from everlasting, my Holy One, my Rock, too pure to look on evil. He reasons from what he knows of God to what he cannot understand, and then he waits. The passage teaches us to hold on to God's revealed character even when His providence baffles us.
basic.originalLanguages: Habakkuk piles up God's names: the Holy One, qadosh, and the Rock, tsur, and says God's eyes are too pure, tahor, to look on evil. These are not doubts about God but the very ground of his complaint. Then he takes his stand at his guard post, mishmereth, the watchman's word, showing that honest questioning ends not in walking away but in waiting on God.
basic.typology: Babylon the insatiable fisherman, dragging in the nations and worshiping his own power, is a picture of every proud human empire that sets itself against God, ultimately unmasked as Babylon the great in Revelation. And the watchman waiting for God's word points to the whole people of God who wait for the sure word and coming of the Lord.
basic.christ: Habakkuk asks how the righteous can be swallowed up by the wicked. At the cross the truly Righteous One, Jesus, was swallowed up by wicked hands, and God brought the greatest good out of the greatest evil. The prophet's struggle finds its deepest answer in a crucified and risen Savior, where God's holiness and His use of evil for good meet.
basic.god: We learn that God is eternal, holy, and utterly pure, a Rock we can lean on even when we cannot trace His ways. We also learn that His holiness is not softness: He will judge the proud who make their strength their god, in His time and by His means.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 73 wrestles with the same puzzle of the wicked prospering. Isaiah 10 shows God using Assyria as His rod, then judging the rod. Revelation 17 to 18 unmasks Babylon the great, the proud world power finally brought down.
basic.oneStory: The prophet's harder question, how can a holy God use the wicked, drives the story deeper into the mystery that God rules over evil without being stained by it, a mystery answered at the cross and completed when proud Babylon falls and the righteous, kept by faith, are vindicated.

context.literary:
This short section is a complaint built like an argument, and its logic runs in a tight chain. Verse 12 states three things Habakkuk knows about God: He is from everlasting, He is the prophet's Holy One, and He has 'appointed' Babylon to execute judgment. Verse 13 then sets beside that confession a premise that seems to contradict it, namely that His eyes cannot look on evil, and draws the question: 'So why do You tolerate the faithless?' The rest of the passage is a defence of why the question is fair. Verses 14 to 17 show what the Chaldean does with the power God gave him, and the passage closes on a question about whether he may 'continue to slay nations without mercy,' 1:17. The prophet does not leave his question to hang. He ends by taking up a watchman's post, 2:1.

The central image is the net. Verses 14 to 16 turn the Babylonian conqueror into a fisherman and the nations into fish. The verbs are rapid and cheerful: he pulls them up, catches them, gathers them, 'so he rejoices gladly.' Then the surprise: he 'sacrifices to his dragnet and burns incense to his fishing net.' The skill that lands the catch becomes the object of worship. The comparison is exact, because a fisherman's whole prosperity depends on his net, and the net itself becomes his god. In the structure of the book this shows how verse 11, 'their own strength is their god,' works out in practice.

The unit has a clear boundary at 2:1, where the speaker changes from address to action. The sentences that had been 'You' sentences, addressed to God, become 'I' sentences: 'I will stand,' 'I will watch,' 'I should answer.' The last verse of the chapter division is thus misleading. Chapter 2 begins in the middle of a single movement, in which the prophet has argued and then waited. The break between chapters comes after the waiting has already begun.

The pairing of complaint and watch also mirrors the previous unit. In the first round Habakkuk spoke and God answered at once. In the second he speaks and is then told to wait, which is a different kind of answer.
context.historical:
The second complaint comes from the same moment as the first, when Babylon is rising and has not yet reached Judah's gates. By about 604 BC the Babylonian army had swept through the coastal plain and destroyed Ashkelon, a sign that the whole region was in its path, and Judah's king Jehoiakim became Nebuchadnezzar's vassal for three years before he rebelled, 2 Kings 24:1. The first deportation, which took the young Daniel and others and some of the temple's vessels, followed, Daniel 1:1 to 2. Habakkuk's questions are being asked by someone who knows what the Babylonian army has done to other cities and expects it to come.

The imagery of fishing and nets was a plain one in the ancient world, and the prophets used it of conquest. Amos warned that Israel's captives would be taken 'with hooks' and 'with fishhooks,' Amos 4:2. Ezekiel spoke of God putting 'hooks in your jaws' and hauling Pharaoh up like a fish, Ezekiel 29:4, and of spreading God's net over him, Ezekiel 32:3. Jeremiah says God will send 'many fishermen' to catch Judah, Jeremiah 16:16. Habakkuk is borrowing a metaphor that his hearers knew, and by making Babylon the fisherman he identifies the empire's role: it is the instrument that hauls peoples in.

The people who first heard the prophet were also asking the question of Judah's survival. 'We will not die' in verse 12 was the confession of a people who believed in the covenant promise to preserve a remnant, and it was a risky thing to say as the Chaldean army approached. Within a generation Jerusalem fell, the temple was burned and many were taken into exile. The confession was not a prediction that no one would die. It was a statement that God's people would not be wiped out.

The watchman's post of 2:1 also belongs to the setting. Cities and borders had lookouts on walls and towers who watched for approaching armies and for messengers, and Isaiah 21:6 to 8 pictures a watchman stationed to report what he sees. Habakkuk takes up the same role, but his enemy is not an army but a delayed word from God.
context.canonical:
The 'from everlasting' of verse 12 is a phrase that carries a good deal of the Bible's weight. The Hebrew word, qedem, appears of God in 'God is my King from ancient times,' Psalm 74:12, and of the eternal God who is 'your dwelling place' in Deuteronomy 33:27. It also appears of the coming Ruler of Bethlehem, 'whose origins are of old, from the days of eternity,' Micah 5:2. The God to whom Habakkuk appeals has the same timeless quality that Micah attributes to the Messiah.

The complaint that a holy God cannot tolerate evil joins other texts that tie His purity to His judgment. 'You are not a God who delights in wickedness; no evil can dwell with You,' Psalm 5:4. Abraham makes the same argument for the righteous in Sodom: 'Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?' Genesis 18:25. Jeremiah brings the same question to God in his own complaint: 'Why does the way of the wicked prosper?' Jeremiah 12:1. These are the great arguments of Scripture's honest wrestlers, and each is built on the character of God.

The fisherman image recurs in the Gospels in a transformed way. Jesus calls His disciples to be 'fishers of men,' Matthew 4:19, and tells of a net cast into the sea that catches all kinds, Matthew 13:47 to 48. The nets that Babylon used for destruction become, in His kingdom, the means of gathering people to Him.

The watchman is a standard office. Ezekiel is 'made a watchman for the house of Israel,' Ezekiel 3:17, and Micah says, 'I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation,' Micah 7:7. Jesus extends the call to all His disciples: 'Keep watch!' Mark 13:37.

The New Testament does not quote these verses directly, but 1 Peter 2:23 and 3:18 describe the Righteous One who was swallowed up by wicked hands and who entrusted Himself to the Judge who judges justly. The question of Habakkuk 1:13, why the righteous are swallowed, is the question the cross answers.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Habakkuk shaped this complaint to teach the people of God how to reason when God's plan collides with God's character. The prophet does not trade one for the other. He asserts both: God is eternal and holy, and God has appointed Babylon. Then he lets the tension stand and asks the question that follows from holding both. The intention is to give believers a way to argue with God that never ends in giving up on Him.

He also wanted his readers to see the moral logic that the empire's success hides. By the standard of a fisherman's profit, the net is a god, because it feeds him. Habakkuk strips that view by naming the offence: the conqueror worships his own cleverness and does not see that the nations are people. The question of 1:17 is not a rhetorical flourish. It asks whether God will let this go on, and it prepares the ground for the woes of chapter 2.

Last, the prophet means to commend the posture of the watchman. He is not announcing that he has an answer. He announces that he is going to wait where an answer can find him. For those who have been told that doubt and faith are enemies, he shows them to be partners, since the one who asks, listens, and the one who listens is ready to be corrected.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage records a prophet's argument, which is not a command to argue with God in every case. What is prescribed is not the complaint itself but the quality of it: it appeals to God's character, it addresses God directly, and it ends in waiting. A person who copies only the questions and leaves out the posture of verse 1 of chapter 2 has not followed the pattern.

The statement that Babylon was appointed 'to execute judgment' should not be turned into a rule that every strong nation is an agent of God. Habakkuk says it of one empire at one time, on the strength of a word from the LORD. He is not saying that whatever happens is what God wants in the same sense. The very next verse presses the objection that God cannot look on evil, and God's answer in chapter 2 will judge the empire.

The comparison of conquest to fishing is a description of how Babylon sees the world, not of how God does. It would be a mistake to take verse 14, 'You have made men like the fish of the sea,' as a claim that humans are cheap. The point is that Babylon has treated them that way, and that the One who made them in His image will not.

debates.question: What does Habakkuk mean when he says the wicked swallow those 'more righteous than themselves'?

views.label: A relative comparison: Judah is better than Babylon
views.case: The Hebrew says the righteous is more righteous 'than he,' a comparative. Habakkuk does not claim Judah is sinless, since he has just complained that Judah's law is paralyzed, 1:4. He claims that Babylon's cruelty exceeds Judah's wrong. On this view the question is about proportion: how can God use the worse to punish the lesser?

views.label: The faithful remnant within Judah
views.case: Others hold that the 'righteous' are the believers inside Judah, such as the prophet himself, who are caught up in the invasion with the guilty. The word the prophet used in 1:4, the righteous hemmed in by the wicked, points to those inside the nation who keep faith. The verse then asks how the righteous can be swallowed by an invader while the guilty are the cause.

debates.bearing: The two views need not exclude each other. Both fit the way the book goes on, with 2:4 pointing to a righteous one who lives by faith in the midst of judgment. The question of verse 13 is answered not by showing that Judah deserved the sentence, but by saying that the righteous live by faith while the proud fall.

debates.question: Does 'We will not die' in verse 12 belong to the original text?

views.label: It is original: a confession of the people's survival
views.case: The Hebrew text read today has 'we will not die,' and the line fits Habakkuk's confidence that God's covenant people will not be wiped out. The preceding clause, 'from everlasting,' grounds that confidence in the covenant LORD who does not change.

views.label: It was altered by scribes from 'You do not die'
views.case: Jewish scribal tradition counts this verse among the places where scribes changed a phrase that seemed irreverent. On that account the original read 'You do not die,' that is, God is immortal, and 'We will not die' replaced it to avoid the thought of God dying even in negation. The reading fits the poetry of the verse, since it follows 'from everlasting,' and it keeps the focus on God.

debates.bearing: The English reader can use either, and no doctrine turns on it. Both readings put the ground of hope in the One who has no beginning and no end, and the book's last verses show a prophet who lives on that ground.

study.originalLanguages:
The phrase 'from everlasting' in verse 12 translates the Hebrew miqqedem, 'from of old, from the earliest time.' The same word stands in Micah 5:2, where the Ruler to come from Bethlehem has origins 'of old, from the days of eternity.' Habakkuk's confession and Micah's promise use one phrase for the age of God and the age of His promised king. Jewish scribal tradition also counts the next words, 'We will not die,' as an alteration of 'You do not die,' lo tamut, which fits the contrast with the everlasting One.

The verb in verse 12 for God's purpose, 'appointed them to execute judgment,' is the verb sim, 'to set, to put in place,' and it is paired with yasad, 'to establish or found,' in 'established them for correction.' The noun there, 'correction,' is a form of the verb yakach, 'to reprove, to argue a case.' The same root returns in 2:1. When Habakkuk says he will watch to see how he should answer 'when corrected,' the Hebrew noun is tokhachti, from the same root, and it can mean 'my complaint' or 'my reproof.' The prophet complains that God has made Babylon the instrument of reproof, and then prepares to be reproved himself. The word has two edges: the prophet is both the one who argues and the one who may be argued with.

In verse 13 the 'faithless' are the bogdim, the treacherous, those who act with betrayal. The verb 'swallow up,' bala, is a strong one, used elsewhere of the earth swallowing Korah and his men, Numbers 16:30. The faithless do not merely defeat the righteous; they devour them whole.

Verse 14 contains a deliberate echo of creation. 'You have made men like the fish of the sea, like creeping things,' uses two terms from Genesis 1:26 to 28, the 'fish of the sea' and the 'creeping thing,' remes. Humanity was made to rule over these creatures. Here humanity itself has been reduced to the status of fish and crawlers that 'have no ruler,' moshel. The prophet implies that someone has to be the shepherd, and that Babylon's net has taken the place of the authority God gave to man over the fish.

Verses 15 and 16 pile up three words for fishing gear, the hook, the dragnet and the net. The vocabulary of verse 16, 'he sacrifices to his dragnet and burns incense,' uses the verbs of the sacrificial system, zavach and qatar, for worship. The conqueror gives to his tool the honours that belong to God.

In 2:1 the watchman's verb is tsafah, 'to watch, to keep a lookout,' the root of the noun tsofeh, 'watchman,' that Ezekiel 3:17 uses when God makes him a watchman. He also takes his stand on the matsor, a fortified or walled place. The same verb of seeing, ra'ah, 'to see,' appears in 'watch to see what He will say to me.' The watchman looks, as God said to look in 1:5, but now his looking is toward God rather than toward the nations.

typology.type: The Rock and Holy One, Habakkuk 1:12
typology.fulfillment: Habakkuk anchors his complaint in God as Holy One and Rock. The New Testament names Christ in the same terms. 'That rock was Christ,' Paul says of the water from the rock in the wilderness, 1 Corinthians 10:4, and the demon cries to Jesus, 'the Holy One of God!' Mark 1:24. The correspondence is that the stability Habakkuk found in God is found, for believers, in the person of Christ. The escalation is that the Rock has become flesh. The type goes only as far as the title: Habakkuk was not seeing Christ in particular, but the New Testament shows that the one he addressed is the one who came.

typology.type: The righteous swallowed by the wicked, Habakkuk 1:13
typology.fulfillment: The question 'Why are You silent while the wicked swallow up those more righteous than themselves?' reaches its fullest case in the cross. The Righteous One was handed over to the lawless, Acts 2:23, and Peter says He suffered 'the righteous for the unrighteous,' 1 Peter 3:18. Before the high priest, 'Jesus remained silent,' Matthew 26:63, fulfilling Isaiah 53:7. The correspondence is that the righteous is swallowed up while God seems to say nothing. The escalation is that God's silence on that day was not abandonment of purpose. It was the way the wicked's act became the means of rescue.

typology.type: The net that gathers the nations, Habakkuk 1:15 to 17
typology.fulfillment: Babylon's net hauls peoples in to destroy them. Jesus uses the same image of His kingdom, saying 'I will make you fishers of men,' Matthew 4:19, and describes a net that gathers all kinds and is sorted at the end, Matthew 13:47 to 48. The relationship is one of contrast: the same instrument, turned to a different end. A net that dragged nations to a conqueror's table now draws people to a Saviour. The type falls short because the kingdom's net is not an act of conquest but of invitation, and the sorting at the end belongs to God, not to the fishers.

Habakkuk takes up a post to watch for God's word. His waiting finds its fulfilment in a church told by Jesus to 'Keep watch!' Mark 13:37, and in a believer's posture of looking to the Lord and waiting for the God of salvation, Micah 7:7. The escalation is that the Master of the house has already come once and promised to come again. The type falls short in that Habakkuk waited for a single word, while the church waits for a person.

study.christ:
Habakkuk's second complaint leads to Christ first by naming God in terms that the New Testament applies to Him. He is the 'Holy One,' and Jesus is called the Holy One of God, Mark 1:24, and the 'Holy and Righteous One,' Acts 3:14. He is the Rock, and Paul says plainly that the rock that accompanied Israel 'was Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:4. And He is 'from everlasting,' the same word used of the Ruler of Bethlehem in Micah 5:2. Habakkuk speaks to the eternal LORD, and the New Testament insists that the eternal One has come among us.

It leads to Christ by the very question the prophet asks. 'Why are You silent while the wicked swallow up those more righteous than themselves?' is a question that Calvary puts at its sharpest. The Righteous One was swallowed by the wicked, 'by the hands of the lawless,' Acts 2:23, and the Father did not intervene. Jesus stood silent before His accusers, Matthew 26:63, and then cried out in the language of the psalm, 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?' Matthew 27:46. Habakkuk's problem, how a holy God can look on evil done to the righteous, is at its most extreme in the death of Jesus. Yet this is where the answer appears. The silence was not the absence of God's purpose. The wicked did what God's 'hand and will had decided beforehand,' Acts 4:28, and it brought forgiveness. As Peter writes, Christ 'suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God,' 1 Peter 3:18.

It leads to Christ by the problem of how God can use evil without being stained by it. At the cross the answer takes a form no prophet could have supplied. God's justice does not simply tolerate wrongdoing. It falls on a substitute. Paul says that God presented Christ as an atoning sacrifice 'so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus,' Romans 3:25 to 26. The holiness that cannot look on evil and the mercy that does not destroy the guilty are brought together there.

It leads to Christ by the fisherman's net. Babylon's net was used to haul nations in for plunder. Jesus takes up the image and reverses it: 'I will make you fishers of men,' Matthew 4:19. The kingdom's net draws people into life, and the sorting at the end is in the hands of God, Matthew 13:47 to 48.

A caution should be made. The fisherman is not a hidden portrait of Satan or of Christ, and the watchman is not a veiled picture of the Messiah. The links here rest on the New Testament's own titles for Jesus, on the way the cross answers the question of verse 13, and on the way Jesus redirects the fishing image.
study.god:
The passage begins by telling us what Habakkuk is sure of, and each item is a doctrine. God is from everlasting: He has no beginning, is not caught by the changes of empires, and sees them from a height that has no date. God is the Holy One: He is set apart in His moral perfection, which is why evil is a problem to Him as well as to us. And God is the Rock: He is the stable foundation under a people whose world is shaking. A believer who is under pressure does well to begin, as the prophet does, with what he knows to be true of God.

Habakkuk's verse 13 says that God's eyes are too pure to look on evil. This is not saying that God does not know about evil. It is saying that He cannot approve it or stand beside it. His purity is not a squeamishness but the heart of His justice. The prophet draws the right conclusion: a God like that cannot be neutral about the wicked swallowing the righteous. The text agrees with Psalm 5:4, 'no evil can dwell with You,' and with Abraham's confidence that the Judge of all the earth will do what is right, Genesis 18:25. God's silence is therefore not approval, and the passage never allows that it might be.

It also shows that God is sovereign in a way that includes real moral distinctions. 'You have appointed them to execute judgment' puts Babylon in God's hand. 'The wicked swallow up those more righteous than themselves' puts Babylon's acts in the category of wickedness. Both are said by the same prophet in the same breath, and the book does not resolve them by diminishing either. God ordains the event and condemns the agent. The way this is possible is not explained here; later Scripture shows it, in Joseph's word to his brothers, 'you intended it for evil, God intended it for good,' Genesis 50:20, and at the cross.

God is a God who can be argued with. The text lets the prophet put the case in the strongest terms and does not rebuke him. This tells us that God values truth over politeness, and that He prefers a questioner who stays in conversation to one who goes silent.

And God is a God who will be waited for. The chapter ends not with a reply but with the prophet on his tower, which assumes that God will speak. The One who is from everlasting is not hurried by the clock of our questions, yet He is not absent from them.

For worship, this means that praise and protest need not be separate, since the prophet's complaint is built from God's own titles. It means that we may pray 'How long?' and 'Why?' without giving up, and that we should post ourselves where His word will find us.

crossReferences.note: The 'from everlasting' of Habakkuk 1:12 uses the same Hebrew word as the Ruler of Bethlehem's origins 'of old.' The eternal God to whom the prophet appeals and the eternal Ruler promised by Micah are linked by the same vocabulary of timeless origin.

Habakkuk 1:14 uses 'fish of the sea' and 'creeping things,' terms from the creation of humanity to rule over such creatures. Babylon has made men themselves like those creatures, which turns the order of creation upside down.

God is not a God who delights in wickedness, and no evil can dwell with Him. The Psalm gives the principle behind verse 13, that the purity of God is the reason the prophet cannot accept the success of the treacherous.
Abraham argues that the Judge of all the earth will do what is right and not treat the righteous like the wicked. Habakkuk is in the same line of those who argue with God from His own character.

Jeremiah brings the same complaint, 'Why does the way of the wicked prosper?' while affirming that God is righteous. It shows that Habakkuk's question was not unique to him but belongs to the prophets of the same period.

Israel's captives would be taken 'with hooks' and 'with fishhooks.' It shows that the fishing image for conquest was already used by the prophets, and that Habakkuk is extending a known picture of what armies did to defeated peoples.

God tells Isaiah to post a lookout who reports what he sees, and the watchman stands day and night on his tower. Habakkuk's resolve in 2:1 follows the same role, with a watch for God's word instead of an army.

God makes Ezekiel a watchman for the house of Israel, who must pass on what he hears from God's mouth. It supplies the office behind Habakkuk's post on the ramparts and shows that a prophet's watching is both for himself and for others.
Jesus calls His followers 'fishers of men,' redeeming the image that Habakkuk used of Babylon. The net that once stood for conquest now stands for the gathering of people to life.

Jesus stood silent before the high priest while the wicked were about to swallow up the Righteous One. His silence fulfils Isaiah 53:7 and puts a human face on the divine silence about which Habakkuk complained.

Christ suffered 'the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God.' The answer to the prophet's question, why the righteous suffer under the wicked, is given in one sentence: because He bore it on behalf of the guilty.

study.oneStory:
The second complaint takes the Bible's oldest question and gives it a sharper form. The question is not only why there is evil but why a holy God can use it, and why the worse seems to prosper over the better. It belongs to a thread that runs from Cain and Abel through Job and the Psalms to Jeremiah, and then on to the cross. Genesis 18:25 sets the principle that the Judge of all the earth will do what is right. Habakkuk presses the case in the hardest circumstances.

The passage looks back to creation in its details. Humanity was made to rule 'the fish of the sea,' Genesis 1:26, and now humanity is netted like fish by one of its own, as though the order of Genesis 1 had been reversed. Nimrod's power and Babel's tower are the first form of the empire that Habakkuk sees in full. The covenant of Genesis 12:3, by which all nations would be blessed, is what Babylon's conquests contradict.

It also looks forward. The questions of 1:12 to 17 are answered in the next chapter by a vision, the waiting of a watchman and the line that the righteous live by faith. The wider canon takes the answer further: Babylon is judged, as Jeremiah 25:12 says, 'when seventy years are complete,' and the exiles return. But the larger question is not answered by return. It is answered by the One who is the Holy One and the Rock and who, as the Righteous One, is swallowed by the wicked and rises. After the cross, the church lives as the watchman does, waiting for the master of the house to return, Mark 13:35 to 37.

The story ends where the prophet's problem ends. In Revelation 18, Babylon, the great fisherman of the nations, falls, and the voice from heaven says, 'Come out of her, My people,' Revelation 18:4. The one who 'sacrifices to his dragnet' is judged, and the cry of the martyrs, 'How long?' Revelation 6:10, is answered in the vindication of Revelation 19:1 to 2. In the new creation the question has no more work to do: there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4, and the Rock on whom Habakkuk leaned will be seen face to face.

sermon.title: Look and Be Amazed!
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in Habakkuk, this message covers Habakkuk 1:5-2:1, including God's answer and the prophet's second complaint that climaxes at the watchtower in 2:1. A faithful, orthodox treatment of the passage of this movement.

quiz.q: What deeper problem does Habakkuk raise in his second complaint?

options.text: How a holy God can use a nation more wicked than Judah to punish it.
options.note: God's first answer, sending Babylon, created a harder question about God's purity.

options.text: Why God stays silent while the wicked swallow up those more righteous than themselves.
options.note: This is exactly his wording, and it is the heart of the puzzle about God's holiness.

options.text: Why God made the sea creatures without a ruler.
options.note: The fish image is a metaphor for helpless nations, not a question about marine life.

options.text: Whether God actually exists at all.
options.note: He never doubts God's existence; he builds on God's holiness and eternity.

quiz.q: On what does Habakkuk base his complaint?

options.text: On God's own character: eternal, holy, the Rock, too pure to look on evil.
options.note: He reasons from what he knows of God to what he cannot understand.

options.text: On God's covenant promise to preserve His people, we will not die.
options.note: This is part of his appeal, but it rests on the deeper ground of God's holy character.

options.text: On his own righteousness compared to God's.
options.note: His appeal is to God's holiness, not his own merit.

options.text: On the idea that God is weak and cannot help.
options.note: He confesses God's eternity and power, not weakness.

quiz.q: What does the image of the fisherman and his net portray?

options.text: Babylon hauling in whole nations and worshiping its own military power.
options.note: He sacrifices to his net, treating his strength as his god.

options.text: The oppressor treating conquered peoples as a helpless catch to be dragged away.
options.note: True to the image, though it misses that he also deifies the net, his own power.

options.text: A call for Judah to take up fishing for a living.
options.note: It is figurative; the fish are conquered peoples caught by Babylon.

options.text: God gathering His people gently to Himself.
options.note: The net here is Babylon's cruelty, not God's care.

quiz.q: What does Habakkuk do at the end of this movement, in 2:1?

options.text: He stations himself on the watchtower to wait for God's reply.
options.note: The watchman's posture of active, expectant waiting for God's word.

options.text: He resolves to listen humbly, ready to be corrected, for how God will answer.
options.note: True to 2:1, though the vivid point is the watchman taking his stand to wait.

options.text: He immediately writes down God's answer.
options.note: The writing of the vision comes in God's reply in 2:2, after he waits.

options.text: He gives up and stops speaking to God.
options.note: The opposite: he takes his stand to wait for an answer.

quiz.q: How does the cross speak to Habakkuk's question about the righteous being swallowed by the wicked?

options.text: The Righteous One, Jesus, was handed to wicked men, and God worked the greatest good from it.
options.note: At Calvary God's holiness and His sovereign use of evil for good meet.

options.text: It shows God can bring great good out of the suffering of the righteous.
options.note: True, and the cross is the supreme case, where the Righteous One is swallowed up for us.

options.text: The cross has nothing to do with Habakkuk's question.
options.note: It is the deepest answer to how the righteous can suffer under the wicked.

options.text: The cross proves that evil always wins in the end.
options.note: The resurrection shows evil is defeated, not victorious.

questions: Habakkuk built his complaint on who God is: eternal, holy, the Rock. When you are confused by life, how might starting with God's character change the way you pray?
God's answer raised a harder question than the one Habakkuk began with. Have you ever found that an answer from God led you deeper into trust rather than tidy closure?
The prophet clung to God as his Rock while everything felt unstable. What does it look like for you to lean on God's unchanging character this week?
Habakkuk ended not by walking away but by climbing his watchtower to wait. Where do you need to move from anxious demanding to expectant waiting on God?
At the cross the truly Righteous One was swallowed up for us. How does that reshape the way you think about your own experiences of injustice?

translationNotes.note: We will not die follows an ancient scribal tradition; the confession rests on God's eternity and covenant faithfulness to preserve His people.
Too pure to look upon evil means God cannot regard wickedness with approval or indifference, not that He is unaware of it; the point is His moral purity.
Guard post and ramparts picture a watchman's station; the prophet takes the posture of one actively watching for God's reply.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Habakkuk 1:12-2:1. Poetic lines rendered as flowing prose within each verse.
